signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.front: What is the single most important step when a child presents with recurrent vomiting?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.back: Characterise the vomit — bilious vs non-bilious, projectile vs effortless, presence of blood, and timing (e.g. early-morning). The character localises the cause and flags dangerous causes to exclude first.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.front: What does BILIOUS (green) vomiting mean until proven otherwise?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.back: Intestinal obstruction — a surgical emergency. Think malrotation with volvulus, intussusception, atresia or incarcerated hernia.Manage with nil by mouth, NG decompression, IV fluids and urgent surgical review/imaging.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.front: A 4-week-old has projectile, non-bilious vomiting and is hungry immediately after feeds. Diagnosis?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.back: Pyloric stenosis (typically presents at 2–8 weeks). A firm 'olive' mass may be palpable; USS confirms. Causes a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis that must be corrected before pyloromyotomy.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.front: What acid-base and electrolyte disturbance is classic for pyloric stenosis?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.back: Hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis (from loss of gastric HCl in the vomit). Correct fluids and electrolytes before surgery.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.front: What triad of features with vomiting should make you suspect raised intracranial pressure / brain tumour?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.back: Early-morning vomiting, headache (worse lying down or on straining) and focal neurology or papilloedema. This is a can't-miss cause — arrange urgent neuroimaging.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.front: What bedside test matters most in a vomiting child, and in whom?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.back: Capillary glucose. Have a low threshold in any vomiting child, and check it in any child with vomiting PLUS thirst, polyuria, weight loss, tiredness, deep breathing or drowsiness.Check ketones if the glucose is raised, in known diabetes, or if a metabolic cause is suspected — not in everyone, since a vomiting child is ketotic from starvation anyway.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.front: How does diabetic ketoacidosis present in a vomiting child?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.back: Vomiting with polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, abdominal pain, dehydration, acidotic (Kussmaul) breathing and drowsiness. Confirm with glucose, ketones and blood gas.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.front: Define cyclical vomiting syndrome.
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.back: Recurrent, stereotyped bouts of intense vomiting lasting hours to days, with complete wellness between, often with a migraine family history.It is a POSITIVE diagnosis made after appropriate evaluation — not simply one of exclusion — but malrotation, raised intracranial pressure, metabolic disease and, in adolescents, cannabinoid hyperemesis and pregnancy must be actively considered.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.front: What is the key clinical hallmark that distinguishes cyclical vomiting syndrome from other recurrent causes?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.back: Stereotyped attacks (each episode is similar) with complete return to normal health between episodes, plus a migraine link/family history.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.front: How is an acute attack of cyclical vomiting syndrome managed?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.back: Quiet dark environment, and rehydration with IV fluid CONTAINING GLUCOSE — fasting ketosis perpetuates the attack, which is the point most often missed.Antiemetics as needed; note ondansetron is off-label here and prolongs the QT interval, so check electrolytes and avoid it in long QT. Identify and avoid triggers, especially fasting and sleep deprivation.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.front: What prophylaxis is used for frequent cyclical vomiting syndrome?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.back: Migraine-type prophylaxis — UK practice has used pizotifen or propranolol — but both are OFF-LABEL for this and specialist-initiated, and there is no UK national guideline.Reserve it for attacks that are frequent or severe.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.front: What is abdominal migraine?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.back: The related midline (periumbilical) abdominal-pain variant of the periodic/migraine-variant syndromes, associated with cyclical vomiting syndrome and a family history of migraine.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.front: What causes effortless posseting in a thriving infant, and how is it managed?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.back: Physiological gastro-oesophageal reflux — it affects over 40% of infants and resolves in about 90% before a year.Reassurance and a feeding review (smaller, more frequent feeds; thickened formula if needed). Do NOT alter the sleeping position for reflux — babies sleep on their back — and do not use acid suppression for regurgitation alone in a well infant.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.front: List the RED FLAG causes of vomiting in a child that must be excluded.
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.back:
• Bilious vomiting (obstruction)
  • raised ICP/brain tumour
  • DKA
  • sepsis/meningitis
  • occult UTI
  • surgical abdomen (appendicitis, intussusception, incarcerated hernia, testicular torsion)
  • severe dehydration
  • faltering growth
  • inborn errors of metabolism
  • and poisoning/ingestion.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.front: Which serious infections commonly present with vomiting as a non-specific early sign?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.back: Sepsis, meningitis and occult urinary tract infection.Vomiting with no obvious focus warrants a clean-catch urine and consideration of a septic screen ± lumbar puncture if meningism.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.front: Why must you always examine the hernial orifices and testes in a vomiting child?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.back: To detect an incarcerated inguinal hernia or testicular torsion — surgical causes of vomiting that are easily missed and where vomiting is typically preceded by pain.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.front: Which recurrent, non-emergency causes of vomiting should be considered in a child?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.back: GORD, cow's milk protein allergy, gastroenteritis/post-viral, chronic infection, overfeeding, and functional/psychogenic vomiting — plus cyclical vomiting syndrome.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.front: What causes of vomiting should specifically be considered in an ADOLESCENT?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.back: Pregnancy, bulimia/rumination and cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (heavy chronic cannabis use with cyclical vomiting relieved by hot showers).

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.front: What metabolic cause should you consider when vomiting occurs with encephalopathy or hypoglycaemia?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.back: An inborn error of metabolism. Investigate with blood gas, glucose, ammonia and metabolic screen.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.front: What key points should the history cover in recurrent childhood vomiting?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.back: Is it bilious, projectile or bloody? Timing (early-morning/on waking)? Triggers? Are episodes stereotyped with wellness between?Headache, polyuria/polydipsia, weight loss, pain preceding the vomit, family history of migraine, growth, diet, and (in adolescents) menstrual and cannabis history.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.front: What must the examination of a vomiting child include?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.back:
• Hydration and perfusion
  • abdomen with hernial orifices and testes
  • fontanelle
  • neurology and fundoscopy (papilloedema)
  • acidotic breathing
  • and growth plotted on a centile chart.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.front: Which investigations are directed by the presentation of recurrent vomiting?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.back:
• Capillary glucose + ketones (DKA) in all
  • U&E (dehydration, pyloric stenosis alkalosis)
  • urine dip & culture (UTI/pregnancy)
  • abdominal USS and surgical review for suspected obstruction
  • and neuroimaging if raised-ICP features.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.front: A child has colicky abdominal pain, redcurrant-jelly stool and a palpable mass. Diagnosis?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.back: Intussusception — a cause of obstruction and (bilious) vomiting. Diagnose with abdominal USS (target/doughnut sign); treat with air/contrast enema reduction or surgery.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.front: Why is early-morning timing of vomiting significant?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.back: Early-morning vomiting, especially with headache, suggests raised intracranial pressure (e.g. brain tumour) — a can't-miss cause requiring neuroimaging.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.front: How does this 'recurrent/cyclical vomiting' topic relate to the other paediatric vomiting topics?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.back: It focuses on the recurrent/cyclical vomiting of the older infant and child. Neonatal/young-infant vomiting and bilious vomiting are covered in separate topics — cross-reference them, remembering bilious vomiting is a surgical emergency.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.front: Which vomiting patterns map to which cause: green, projectile non-bilious, effortless, bloody?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.back:
• Green (bilious) = obstruction
  • projectile non-bilious at 2–8 weeks = pyloric stenosis
  • effortless posseting = GORD
  • blood = Mallory-Weiss tear, oesophagitis or a serious cause.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.front: What is the acute versus preventive approach to cyclical vomiting in one line?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Vomiting in.back: Acute: glucose-containing IV fluid, a quiet dark room, antiemetics (ondansetron off-label, watch the QT).Preventive: trigger avoidance, and off-label specialist-initiated pizotifen or propranolol if attacks are frequent or severe.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.front: How is recurrent (chronic) abdominal pain in a child classically defined?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.back: At least 3 episodes of abdominal pain over a period of at least 3 months, severe enough to interrupt normal activity (Apley's original definition).

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.front: In a school-age child with recurrent abdominal pain, is an organic or functional cause more likely?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.back: Functional is far more likely — the majority have no identifiable organic cause. The aim is to make a positive functional diagnosis while excluding organic disease.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.front: What is Apley's rule — and how much weight should it carry?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.back: 'The further the pain is from the umbilicus, the more likely it is organic.'Treat it as a rough HEURISTIC, not a rule: it has never been validated, young children localise pain poorly, and pain location was dropped from the modern consensus criteria.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.front: Name the four Rome IV functional abdominal pain disorders in children.
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.back:
• Functional abdominal pain
  • irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)
  • functional dyspepsia
  • and abdominal migraine.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.front: What are the typical features of functional abdominal pain?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.back: Periumbilical pain, no red flags, normal growth and examination, often linked to stress/anxiety and school avoidance. Made as a positive Rome IV diagnosis.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.front: How does IBS present in a child?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.back: Abdominal pain relieved by defecation, with altered stool form and/or frequency; bloating and mucus; symptoms fluctuate with stress and diet.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.front: What characterises functional dyspepsia?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.back: Epigastric, meal-related pain with early satiety, nausea and bloating, and no alarm features. Consider H. pylori / peptic disease if persistent.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.front: What are the hallmark features of abdominal migraine?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.back: Episodic midline abdominal pain with pallor, nausea and anorexia; the child is completely well between attacks; personal or family history of migraine.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.front: How is abdominal migraine managed?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.back: Reassurance and trigger management first — regular meals, sleep, hydration.Drug prophylaxis such as pizotifen is OFF-LABEL, second-line and specialist-initiated, for frequent or disabling attacks only, and rests on a single small trial.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.front: List key red flags suggesting an organic cause of recurrent abdominal pain.
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.back:
• Faltering growth/weight loss
  • GI bleeding
  • nocturnal pain or diarrhoea waking the child
  • persistent or bilious vomiting
  • dysphagia
  • fever
  • joint symptoms
  • perianal disease
  • FHx IBD/coeliac
  • pain away from the umbilicus
  • dysuria
  • and organomegaly/mass.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.front: Why is constipation important in recurrent abdominal pain?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.back: It is a very common organic cause — infrequent hard painful stools, overflow soiling and a palpable faecal mass.Diagnosis is clinical; do a proper abdominal exam and treat with laxatives/disimpaction.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.front: Which organic conditions should routinely be excluded in recurrent abdominal pain?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.back: Constipation, urinary tract infection, coeliac disease and inflammatory bowel disease — all common, easy to miss and cheap to exclude.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.front: What features point towards inflammatory bowel disease?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.back: Older child/adolescent with weight loss, bloody diarrhoea, lethargy, perianal disease, mouth ulcers, arthralgia and a family history of IBD; raised faecal calprotectin.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.front: Which test screens for IBD in a child, and what is the age caveat?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.back: Faecal calprotectin, in a child with SUSPECTED IBD referred for specialist assessment — not as a screen for every child with tummy ache.It is physiologically high in infants and only reaches adult-type values around 4 years, so results below that age are hard to interpret, and it is raised non-specifically by infection and NSAIDs.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.front: How is coeliac disease screened for?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.back: Coeliac serology — anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-tTG) IgA with a total IgA level (to exclude IgA deficiency); confirmed on duodenal biopsy while on a gluten-containing diet.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.front: What must always be considered in an adolescent girl with recurrent/lower abdominal pain?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.back: Gynaecological causes — ovarian pathology, dysmenorrhoea, ectopic pregnancy — and a pregnancy test should be done where relevant.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.front: Why must appendicitis be reconsidered in a child with recurrent abdominal pain?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.back: Chronic functional pain can become acute-on-chronic surgical pathology; localised RIF pain with guarding, or bilious vomiting, means appendicitis or obstruction — never anchor on a functional label.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.front: What basic investigations may be used to exclude organic disease when indicated?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.back:
• Urinalysis and culture
  • FBC/CRP/ESR
  • coeliac serology
  • faecal calprotectin (if IBD suspected)
  • and a pregnancy test in adolescents.
Investigate only when history/red flags indicate.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.front: What does a normal examination and normal growth in a well child suggest?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.back: It strongly supports a functional cause — growth and examination are characteristically normal in functional abdominal pain.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.front: What are the core elements of managing functional abdominal pain?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.back: A positive explanation and reassurance, addressing psychosocial stressors, encouraging normal school attendance, and dietary review.For psychological therapy, GUT-DIRECTED HYPNOTHERAPY has the strongest evidence, with CBT close behind.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.front: What dietary approach is used for childhood IBS?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.back: First-line is regular meals, adequate fibre and fluid, and cutting excess fruit juice and fizzy drinks. A low-FODMAP diet is NOT routinely recommended in children — the evidence is from adults, and restriction risks nutritional inadequacy and disordered eating.Reserve it for selected adolescents under specialist paediatric dietetic supervision, time-limited with structured reintroduction.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.front: Why is encouraging normal school attendance important in functional abdominal pain?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.back: Pain is often linked to stress/anxiety and school avoidance; reinforcing avoidance perpetuates the symptom. Maintaining normal activity and school is central to recovery.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.front: What is the danger of over-investigating a child with a positive functional picture?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.back: Excessive tests reinforce illness behaviour, cause anxiety, and can do harm without benefit. A positive diagnosis should be made rather than relying on endless exclusion.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.front: Where is functional abdominal pain typically felt, and why does that matter?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.back: It is typically central/periumbilical. By Apley's rule, pain located away from the umbilicus is more likely to have an organic cause and warrants closer scrutiny.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.front: Which nocturnal symptoms are red flags in recurrent abdominal pain?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.back: Pain or diarrhoea that wakes the child from sleep — functional symptoms rarely wake a child, so nocturnal features point towards organic disease (e.g. IBD).

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.front: What is the significance of bilious (green) vomiting in a child?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.back: It is a red flag for intestinal obstruction (e.g. malrotation with volvulus) and requires urgent surgical assessment — not a functional feature.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.front: Summarise the exam-favourite pearls for recurrent abdominal pain in a child.
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Recurrent Abdominal P.back:
• Most is functional
  • Apley's rule (further from umbilicus = more organic)
  • exclude constipation, UTI, coeliac and IBD
  • know the red flags
  • recognise abdominal migraine (episodic + pallor + migraine link)
  • pregnancy test in adolescent girls
  • treat with positive diagnosis, normal school attendance and CBT.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.front: What is the single most important priority when assessing a child with acute diarrhoea?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.back: Assess and manage DEHYDRATION. Grade as no clinically detectable dehydration, clinical dehydration, or clinical shock, and rehydrate (ORS first-line, IV fluids for shock).

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.front: What is the commonest cause of acute diarrhoea in a child?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.back: Viral gastroenteritis. Since the rotavirus immunisation programme, NOROVIRUS is the leading viral cause in UK children; rotavirus still circulates but is far less common — think of it in the unimmunised.The task is to assess and treat dehydration, not to give antibiotics.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.front: List the main bacterial causes of gastroenteritis in children.
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.back:
• Campylobacter
  • Salmonella
  • Shigella
  • and E. coli (including E. coli O157).
Parasitic causes include Giardia.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.front: Which gastroenteritis pathogen carries a risk of haemolytic uraemic syndrome?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.back: Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) — classically O157, though other serogroups such as O26 now account for a large share of UK cases, so think STEC rather than O157 alone. Shigella too.Antibiotics AND antimotility agents are both avoided, as they increase HUS risk.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.front: What is first-line treatment for clinical dehydration in a child with gastroenteritis?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.back: Oral rehydration solution (ORS) - typically 50 mL/kg over 4 hours plus maintenance, given little and often (NG tube if not tolerated orally). Continue breastfeeding.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.front: When are IV fluids indicated in a child with diarrhoea, and at what volume?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.back: In clinical shock, or when the child cannot tolerate or fails oral/NG rehydration. The bolus is 10 mL/kg of crystalloid over less than 10 minutes, reassessed and repeated as needed — UK guidance moved from 20 to 10 mL/kg, so older sources will say 20.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.front: Should antidiarrhoeals and antibiotics be routinely used in childhood gastroenteritis?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.back: No. Do NOT routinely use antidiarrhoeals or antibiotics. Antibiotics are reserved for specific pathogens, sepsis, or immunocompromise - and are avoided in E. coli O157.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.front: List the clinical signs of dehydration in a child.
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.back:
• Reduced urine output
  • dry mucous membranes
  • sunken eyes
  • reduced skin turgor
  • sunken fontanelle
  • tachycardia
  • irritability/lethargy.
Shock adds prolonged capillary refill, cold mottled extremities, weak pulses and (late) hypotension.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.front: Why is hypotension a dangerous sign in a dehydrated child?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.back: It is a LATE, pre-terminal sign of shock in children - they compensate well until they decompensate suddenly. Act on tachycardia and prolonged capillary refill before blood pressure falls.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.front: What are the key red flags in a child with diarrhoea?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.back:
• Signs of shock/severe dehydration
  • blood in the stool
  • bilious (green) vomiting
  • a septic/unwell child
  • faltering growth/weight loss
  • marked abdominal distension or severe pain
  • and immunocompromise.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.front: What does bilious (green) vomiting in a child suggest?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.back: Bowel obstruction until proven otherwise - a surgical emergency. Keep nil by mouth, image, and refer to surgery.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.front: What is the tetrad of haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS)?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.back:
• Bloody diarrhoea (often after E. coli O157)
  • followed by acute kidney injury (AKI)
  • microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia
  • and thrombocytopenia.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.front: How is HUS managed, and what must be avoided?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.back: Supportive care (fluid/electrolyte management, may need renal replacement therapy). AVOID antibiotics and antimotility agents, which increase HUS risk.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.front: What features suggest intussusception in a child with diarrhoea?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.back: Paroxysmal severe colic (drawing up legs), redcurrant-jelly stool, a sausage-shaped abdominal mass, and vomiting. Confirm with abdominal ultrasound.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.front: How do you distinguish acute from chronic diarrhoea?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.back: Acute is <2 weeks (usually infective/gastroenteritis); chronic is ≥2-4 weeks and warrants a work-up for causes such as coeliac, IBD, CF, or toddler's diarrhoea.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.front: What is toddler's diarrhoea (chronic nonspecific diarrhoea)?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.back: The commonest cause of chronic diarrhoea in a WELL, thriving toddler (6 months-5 years): loose stools with undigested food ('peas and carrots'), normal growth. Reassure; resolves by school age.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.front: What are the '4 Fs' associated with toddler's diarrhoea?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.back:
• Excess Fruit juice
  • low Fat
  • abnormal Fibre
  • and excess Fluid intake.
Dietary adjustment of these often improves symptoms.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.front: What chronic causes of diarrhoea present with faltering growth?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.back: Coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), and cystic fibrosis (CF).Faltering growth rules OUT toddler's diarrhoea and mandates investigation.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.front: How is coeliac disease screened for in a child?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.back: Anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA PLUS a total IgA — the total IgA is separate, and is there to catch IgA deficiency causing a false negative. It is only valid on a gluten-containing diet (more than one meal a day for at least 6 weeks).Positive serology goes to paediatric gastroenterology.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.front: What features suggest inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) as a cause of diarrhoea?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.back: An older child with blood in stool, weight loss, abdominal pain, and a raised faecal calprotectin. Diagnosis is confirmed with endoscopy/biopsy.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.front: How does cystic fibrosis cause diarrhoea?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.back: Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency causes malabsorption with steatorrhoea (fatty, offensive stools) plus faltering growth and recurrent respiratory infections. Diagnosed with the sweat test/genetics.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.front: What is overflow diarrhoea, and why is it a common trap?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.back: Chronic constipation with faecal impaction causes liquid stool to leak around the mass (soiling/loose stool), mimicking diarrhoea. Always do an abdominal +/- PR/perineal examination to detect it.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.front: What is post-infectious lactose intolerance?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.back: Transient lactase deficiency after an episode of gastroenteritis causing continued loose stools; usually self-limiting and resolves as the gut mucosa recovers.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.front: Which investigations are indicated in a child with diarrhoea, and when?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.back:
Often none in simple gastroenteritis. Directed:
  • stool culture/microscopy (blood, prolonged, systemic, travel)
  • U&E (dehydration/HUS)
  • FBC & film (HUS)
  • coeliac serology (anti-TTG+IgA)
  • faecal calprotectin (IBD)
  • blood glucose/gas if unwell.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.front: What history points to viral gastroenteritis rather than a serious cause?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.back: Watery (non-bloody) diarrhoea +/- vomiting, low-grade fever, sick contacts, and a child who is well between episodes with normal growth.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.front: When are antibiotics justified in childhood gastroenteritis?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.back: For specific identified pathogens where treatment is indicated, in sepsis, or in the immunocompromised child. They should NOT be given routinely, and never in suspected E. coli O157.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.front: What is the guideline framework underpinning management of gastroenteritis and dehydration in children?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.back: NICE CG84 (diarrhoea and vomiting in children under 5) / NICE CKS - assess dehydration clinically, rehydrate with ORS first-line, and reserve antibiotics for specific indications.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.front: Summarise the exam-favourite approach to a child with diarrhoea.
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Diarrhoea in a Child.back:
• Acute diarrhoea = usually viral gastroenteritis - assess/treat dehydration with ORS, avoid antibiotics (especially O157/HUS).
  • Toddler's diarrhoea = well thriving child, undigested food, '4 Fs', resolves by school age.
  • Chronic + faltering growth = coeliac/IBD/CF.
  • Exclude overflow constipation.
  • Blood, bilious vomiting or shock are red flags.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.front: How should you frame the excessively crying / unsettled infant?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.back: As an APPROACH, not a single disease. Crying is a symptom: first EXCLUDE a serious cause, then diagnose infantile colic (a diagnosis of exclusion) and support the family.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.front: Define infantile colic (the 'rule of 3s').
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.back: Crying at least 3 hours/day, at least 3 days/week, for at least 1 WEEK, in a well, thriving infant; peaks around 6 weeks and resolves by 3–4 months.Note older texts say 3 WEEKS — UK guidance now uses one week, and the international consensus has dropped the arbitrary thresholds for 'starts and stops before 5 months'.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.front: Why is colic described as a 'diagnosis of exclusion'?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.back: Because it can only be diagnosed in a well, thriving baby AFTER a careful history and a thorough top-to-toe examination have excluded serious, treatable causes of crying.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.front: What serious infective causes must be excluded in a crying baby?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.back: Sepsis and meningitis (fever OR hypothermia, poor feeding, lethargy, bulging fontanelle, high-pitched cry), occult UTI, and otitis media.A crying, unwell/febrile infant needs a full septic screen and a urine check.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.front: What are the key surgical abdominal causes of inconsolable crying?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.back:
• Intussusception
  • incarcerated inguinal hernia
  • testicular/ovarian torsion
  • and malrotation/volvulus.
Bilious (green) vomiting is a volvulus/malrotation until proven otherwise.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.front: Describe the classic presentation of intussusception.
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.back: Episodic inconsolable crying with drawing-up of the legs, pallor and vomiting, later redcurrant-jelly stool and a sausage-shaped abdominal mass. Confirmed on abdominal ultrasound (target/doughnut sign).

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.front: Why must every crying baby be FULLY UNDRESSED and examined?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.back:
To find hidden physical causes:
  • a hair/thread tourniquet on a finger, toe or penis
  • a strangulated hernia or torsion
  • corneal abrasion
  • an open nappy pin
  • bruising
  • or a limb that won't move (occult fracture).

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.front: What is a hair/thread tourniquet and where do you look for it?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.back: A strand of hair or thread wound tightly around a digit or the penis, causing a swollen, discoloured, painful appendage. Inspect every finger and toe and the penis in an inconsolable baby.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.front: How does non-accidental injury (NAI) relate to a crying baby?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.back: Crying is a recognised TRIGGER for abusive head trauma (shaking). Also consider occult fracture (a baby who won't move a limb), bruising in a non-mobile infant, and an inconsistent or delayed history.Keep NAI in mind in every crying baby.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.front: What features suggest cow's milk protein allergy as the cause?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.back: Poor weight gain, blood or mucus in the stool, eczema and atopic family history are the discriminating ones.Feeding distress, back-arching and regurgitation are highly non-specific and overlap with normal reflux and colic — which is why CMPA is over-diagnosed.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.front: What features suggest GORD (reflux) in a crying infant?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.back: Feeding-related distress, regurgitation/vomiting and back-arching. Assessed alongside CMPA as a feeding-related cause once serious pathology is excluded.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.front: When should the urine be checked in a crying infant?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.back: If there is fever ≥38°C, or if an infant under 3 months is also feeding poorly, vomiting, lethargic or failing to gain — NOT routinely in a well, afebrile, thriving baby.Under 3 months do not use a dipstick: send urgent microscopy and culture.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.front: What non-infective, non-surgical causes should be considered in a crying baby?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.back: Raised intracranial pressure (bulging fontanelle), a cardiac cause such as SVT (check the heart rate), and metabolic causes - in addition to corneal abrasion and other hidden physical causes.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.front: What must the history in a crying baby cover?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.back:
• Pattern/timing of crying
  • feeding
  • vomiting (bilious? projectile?)
  • stool (blood/mucus/redcurrant jelly)
  • fever
  • wet nappies/urine output
  • birth and developmental history
  • and parental coping/mental health.
Note any inconsistent or delayed history.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.front: What does a top-to-toe examination of the undressed infant include?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.back:
• Temperature and observations
  • anterior fontanelle
  • ears (otoscopy)
  • eyes (fluorescein for corneal abrasion)
  • chest
  • abdomen with hernial orifices and genitalia/scrotum
  • every digit and the penis for a tourniquet
  • tone and limb movement
  • skin
  • and plotting growth.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.front: What investigations may a crying baby need?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.back:
Often none in a well baby. Urine if febrile or if under 3 months with poor feeding, vomiting or lethargy. If febrile and under 3 months:
  • FBC, CRP, blood culture and urine in all
  • LP in every infant under 1 month, and at 1–3 months if unwell or the white cell count is below 5 or above 15
  • CXR only if there are respiratory signs.
Abdominal USS if intussusception is suspected.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.front: Once serious causes are excluded, what is the first step in managing colic?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.back: Reassurance and explanation that colic is common, benign and self-limiting, resolving by ~3-4 months; plus a feeding review and advice on soothing techniques (holding, motion, winding, a calm environment).

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.front: Are simeticone and lactase drops recommended for colic?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.back: No. Simeticone and lactase drops are NOT recommended for infantile colic because there is no good evidence they work.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.front: When might a hydrolysed formula or maternal dairy exclusion be tried?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.back: Only as a time-limited trial of about 2–4 weeks when cow's milk protein allergy is genuinely suspected — and it MUST be followed by planned reintroduction to confirm or refute it, the step most often skipped.Use an EXTENSIVELY hydrolysed formula; a lactose-free formula is not a treatment for CMPA, and soya is not used under 6 months.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.front: Why is supporting parental wellbeing central to managing a crying baby?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.back: Because crying is a recognised trigger for parental frustration and abusive head trauma.Advise parents to never shake the baby, to put the baby down safely and take a break if overwhelmed, and safety-net clearly.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.front: What safety advice should every parent of a crying baby receive?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.back:
• Never shake the baby
  • if overwhelmed, put the baby down somewhere safe and step away to calm down
  • and return/seek help urgently if the baby develops fever, poor feeding, drowsiness, vomiting (especially bilious) or any new concern.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.front: Give three 'red flag' features that mean crying is NOT colic.
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.back:
Any of:
  • fever or hypothermia
  • poor feeding/lethargy
  • bulging fontanelle
  • bilious or projectile vomiting
  • faltering growth
  • blood in stool
  • a swollen digit/penis
  • or a limb that won't move.
Colic requires a well, thriving baby.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.front: What is the typical time course of infantile colic?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.back: Onset in the early weeks, peaking at around 6 weeks of age, and usually resolving spontaneously by 3-4 months.Often worst in the evening ('witching hour') with the baby red-faced and legs drawn up.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.front: Why does bilious (green) vomiting in a crying infant demand urgent action?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.back: It suggests intestinal malrotation with volvulus, a surgical emergency threatening bowel viability - it is a volvulus until proven otherwise and needs immediate surgical assessment.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.front: How is a UTI confirmed in a febrile infant with no focus?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.back: Urine culture. In an infant under 3 months do NOT rely on a dipstick — send urgent microscopy and culture and involve paediatrics, because nitrite is unreliable at this age and the signs are non-specific.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.front: Summarise the exam-pearl approach to the crying baby in one line.
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Crying Baby / Infanti.back: Colic = rule of 3s in a WELL, thriving baby and is a diagnosis of EXCLUSION; always fully undress and examine (hair tourniquet, hernia, corneal abrasion), exclude sepsis/UTI/intussusception/NAI, avoid simeticone/lactase, and support parents (never shake).

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Fever in a Child.front: How is fever defined in a child, and what is the first framework to use?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Fever in a Child.back: A temperature ≥38°C. Use the NICE traffic-light system (colour, activity, respiratory, circulation / hydration, other) to grade the risk of serious illness.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Fever in a Child.front: What must you assume in a febrile child with a non-blanching rash?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Fever in a Child.back: Meningococcal septicaemia until proven otherwise — give parenteral antibiotics immediately and treat for sepsis; do not wait for investigations.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Fever in a Child.front: Why is fever in an infant under 3 months high-risk?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Fever in a Child.back: Serious bacterial infection is far more likely and signs are non-specific; a temperature ≥38°C mandates a full septic screen (blood, urine, CSF ± CXR) and admission.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Fever in a Child.front: Which features of meningitis are non-specific in a young infant?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Fever in a Child.back: Irritability, poor feeding, high-pitched cry, drowsiness and a bulging fontanelle — classic neck stiffness / photophobia may be absent.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Fever in a Child.front: What should you always send in a febrile child with no obvious focus?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Fever in a Child.back: A urine sample (clean-catch) for dipstick and culture — UTI is a common occult cause of fever, especially in infants.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Fever in a Child.front: What defines Kawasaki disease and why does it matter?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Fever in a Child.back: Fever ≥5 days plus conjunctivitis, mucositis (cracked lips / strawberry tongue), rash, extremity changes and cervical nodeit risks coronary artery aneurysms, so needs echo and IVIG + aspirin.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Fever in a Child.front: What are the key red (high-risk) traffic-light features?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Fever in a Child.back:
• Pale / mottled / cyanosed
  • no response to social cues
  • weak / high-pitched cry
  • grunting
  • tachypnoea
  • reduced skin turgor
  • non-blanching rash
  • bulging fontanelle
  • neck stiffness
  • status / focal seizures
  • age <3 months with fever.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Fever in a Child.front: What is the immediate management of the septic febrile child?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Fever in a Child.back: Sepsis 6: high-flow oxygen, IV / IO access with blood cultures and lactate, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, IV fluid bolus, and monitor urine output — escalate to seniors.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Fever in a Child.front: Does a good response to antipyretics exclude serious illness?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Fever in a Child.back: No — response to antipyretics does not reliably distinguish serious from self-limiting illness; assess the whole clinical picture.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Fever in a Child.front: A febrile child with cough, tachypnoea and chest recession most likely has what?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Fever in a Child.back: A lower respiratory tract infection / pneumonia; assess work of breathing and oxygen saturation and consider a CXR if indicated.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Fever in a Child.front: What is the significance of fever with a limp or refusal to weight-bear?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Fever in a Child.back: It raises septic arthritis or osteomyelitis — a bone / joint infection needing urgent assessment (inflammatory markers, aspiration).

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Fever in a Child.front: What is appropriate for the well, low-risk (green) febrile child?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Fever in a Child.back: Reassurance with clear safety-netting advice on warning signs, fluids and when to re-present, rather than admission or extensive investigation.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Rash in a Child.front: What is the single most important first question about a childhood rash?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Rash in a Child.back: Does it blanch? A non-blanching rash in an unwell, febrile child is meningococcal until proven otherwise and takes priority over morphology.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Rash in a Child.front: Which rash plus systemic features is a medical emergency requiring adrenaline?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Rash in a Child.back: Urticaria with angioedema (lip / tongue swelling), wheeze, stridor or hypotension — this is anaphylaxis, treated with IM adrenaline.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Rash in a Child.front: Describe the rash and pathognomonic sign of measles.
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Rash in a Child.back: A maculopapular rash spreading from behind the ears / face downwards, with preceding coryza, conjunctivitis, fever and Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa.
Itchy vesicles appearing in crops, so lesions are at different stages (macule → papule → vesicle → crust) simultaneously.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Rash in a Child.front: What causes slapped-cheek syndrome and what is a key risk?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Rash in a Child.back: Parvovirus B19; it causes bright red cheeks then a lacy limb rash, and risks aplastic crisis in sickle cell disease and hydrops in pregnancy.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Rash in a Child.front: What are the features and management of atopic eczema?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Rash in a Child.back: An itchy, dry, flexural rash in an atopic child; managed with emollients and topical corticosteroids, treating flares and infection (watch for eczema herpeticum).

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Rash in a Child.front: What is scarlet fever and how is it recognised?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Rash in a Child.back: A group A streptococcal illness with a sandpaper-like rash, flushed cheeks with circumoral pallor, strawberry tongue and sore throat; it is notifiable and treated with antibiotics.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Rash in a Child.front: What is impetigo and how does it present?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Rash in a Child.back: A superficial bacterial skin infection (staph / strep) causing honey-coloured crusted lesions, often around the mouth/nose; treated with topical or oral antibiotics.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Rash in a Child.front: What are the classic features of Henoch-Schönlein purpura?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Rash in a Child.back: Palpable purpura over the extensor legs and buttocks, arthralgia, colicky abdominal pain and IgA nephritis, with normal platelets; monitor BP and urinalysis.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Rash in a Child.front: Which rashes should prompt a safeguarding assessment?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Rash in a Child.back:
• Patterned bruising
  • cigarette-type burns
  • bruising in a non-mobile infant
  • or marks inconsistent with the history.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Rash in a Child.front: What is eczema herpeticum and why does it matter?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Rash in a Child.back: A herpes simplex infection of eczematous skin causing painful, punched-out monomorphic lesions in an unwell child — a dermatological emergency needing aciclovir.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Rash in a Child.front: Which viral exanthems are notifiable in the UK?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Rash in a Child.back: Measles, rubella and mumps (and scarlet fever, a streptococcal illness) must be notified to public health.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Non-Blanching Rash.front: What does a non-blanching rash signify and how is it tested?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Non-Blanching Rash.back: Blood has extravasated from vessels (petechiae / purpura); it is confirmed with the tumbler / glass test — the rash persists under pressure.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Non-Blanching Rash.front: What is the overriding diagnosis in a febrile child with a non-blanching rash?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Non-Blanching Rash.back: Meningococcal septicaemia until proven otherwise — give parenteral antibiotics and treat for sepsis without waiting for investigations.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Non-Blanching Rash.front: How does the presence of fever change the differential of a non-blanching rash?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Non-Blanching Rash.back: Febrile / unwell points to meningococcal sepsis (and DIC); afebrile / well points to HSP, ITP, mechanical petechiae — but always exclude leukaemia and NAI.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Non-Blanching Rash.front: How is HSP distinguished from ITP on the blood count?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Non-Blanching Rash.back: HSP has a normal platelet count (it is a vasculitis); ITP has isolated thrombocytopenia with an otherwise normal count.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Non-Blanching Rash.front: What is the typical story of ITP in a child?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Non-Blanching Rash.back: A well child with isolated thrombocytopenia causing petechiae, bruising and mucosal bleeding, often 1-2 weeks after a viral infection; usually self-limiting.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Non-Blanching Rash.front: Which features of a non-blanching rash suggest leukaemia?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Non-Blanching Rash.back:
• Petechiae / bruising with pallor
  • fatigue
  • fever
  • bone pain
  • hepatosplenomegaly
  • lymphadenopathy and other cytopenias on the blood count.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Non-Blanching Rash.front: When is a non-blanching rash a safeguarding concern?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Non-Blanching Rash.back: Bruising or petechiae in a non-mobile infant, patterned marks, unusual sites (ears, torso, buttocks) or a history inconsistent with the injuries — inflicted until proven otherwise.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Non-Blanching Rash.front: What causes benign mechanical petechiae and how are they distributed?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Non-Blanching Rash.back: Forceful coughing, vomiting or crying raise SVC pressure, causing petechiae confined above the nipple line / SVC in a well child with a normal blood count.
Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury, classically after bloody diarrhoea (E. coli O157).

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Non-Blanching Rash.front: What initial investigations are needed for a non-blanching rash?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Non-Blanching Rash.back:
• FBC and blood film
  • coagulation screen
  • U&E and urinalysis
  • CRP / blood culture and meningococcal PCR if febrile
skeletal survey if NAI is suspected.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Non-Blanching Rash.front: Why must you not delay antibiotics in suspected meningococcal septicaemia?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Non-Blanching Rash.back: Delay increases mortality; the rash can evolve from petechial to purpuric within hours as the child becomes septic and develops DIC.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Non-Blanching Rash.front: What is disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) in this context?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Non-Blanching Rash.back: Widespread activation of clotting causing consumption of platelets and clotting factors, giving purpura and bleeding — seen in severe sepsis such as meningococcal disease.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Limp in a Child.front: What is the must-not-miss cause of a limp in a febrile child?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Limp in a Child.back: Septic arthritis or osteomyelitis — a child who refuses to weight-bear with fever needs urgent assessment, aspiration and antibiotics.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Limp in a Child.front: What are Kocher's criteria and their use?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Limp in a Child.back: Fever >38.5°C, non-weight-bearing, ESR >40 and WCC >12more criteria increase the probability of septic arthritis over transient synovitis.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Limp in a Child.front: How does the differential for a limp vary with age?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Limp in a Child.back:
• Infant / toddler → DDH
  • 3-10 years → transient synovitis or Perthes
  • adolescent → SUFE
  • any age → septic arthritis, malignancy, trauma / NAI.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Limp in a Child.front: What features of a limp suggest malignancy?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Limp in a Child.back: Bone pain that wakes the child at night, pallor, bruising, fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy — consider leukaemia or a bone tumour.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Limp in a Child.front: What is transient synovitis and how is it diagnosed?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Limp in a Child.back: A self-limiting post-viral hip irritability in a well child aged 3-10 who can usually weight-bear; a diagnosis of exclusion once septic arthritis is ruled out.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Limp in a Child.front: Who gets SUFE and how does it present?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Limp in a Child.back: Typically an overweight adolescent; with hip or referred knee pain, an externally rotated leg and loss of internal rotation; confirmed on a frog-leg lateral X-ray.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Limp in a Child.front: How does developmental dysplasia of the hip present in an infant?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Limp in a Child.back: Asymmetric skin creases, limited hip abduction, leg-length discrepancy and a positive Barlow / Ortolani in the newborn; a waddling gait if walking.
Idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head, usually in boys aged 4-8, causing insidious hip pain, a limp and limited internal rotation; X-ray both hips.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Limp in a Child.front: When should juvenile idiopathic arthritis be suspected in a limping child?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Limp in a Child.back: With persistent joint swelling and stiffness for more than 6 weeks, morning stiffness and no infection.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Limp in a Child.front: What imaging is used for SUFE and for suspected DDH?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Limp in a Child.back: SUFE: frog-leg (lateral) X-ray of the hips. DDH: ultrasound under about 4.5 months, then X-ray once the femoral head ossifies.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Limp in a Child.front: What is the emergency management of septic arthritis?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Limp in a Child.back: Urgent joint aspiration for microscopy and culture, IV antibiotics and orthopaedic referral for washout — delay risks joint destruction and avascular necrosis.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Limp in a Child.front: Why must a frog-leg X-ray be done for suspected SUFE even if the child complains only of knee pain?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Limp in a Child.back: Hip pathology commonly refers pain to the knee; a missed SUFE progresses to slip and permanent deformity / avascular necrosis.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Vomiting in a Neonate.front: What is the significance of bilious (green) vomiting in a neonate?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Vomiting in a Neonate.back: It is intestinal obstruction — malrotation with midgut volvulus — until proven otherwise; a surgical emergency needing urgent contrast study and referral.
Volvulus can twist the midgut around the superior mesenteric vessels and infarct the entire small bowel within hours.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Vomiting in a Neonate.front: What are the classic features of pyloric stenosis?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Vomiting in a Neonate.back: Projectile, non-bilious vomiting at 4-8 weeks in a hungry baby, with visible peristalsis and a palpable olive, causing a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.
Correct the fluid and electrolyte (alkalosis) disturbance first, then perform a Ramstedt pyloromyotomy.
A child of 3 months-2 years (peak 5-9 months) with colicky pain (drawing up the legs), pallor, a sausage-shaped mass and redcurrant-jelly stool; confirmed on ultrasound (target sign).
Reduction with an air (or contrast) enema; surgery if the enema fails or there is peritonitis / perforation.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Vomiting in a Neonate.front: What features of vomiting suggest sepsis in an infant?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Vomiting in a Neonate.back: Lethargy, poor feeding, temperature instability, apnoea and poor perfusion — screen and give antibiotics.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Vomiting in a Neonate.front: What is necrotising enterocolitis and who is at risk?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Vomiting in a Neonate.back: Bowel inflammation and necrosis, mainly in preterm infants, causing bilious vomiting, abdominal distension and bloody stool; managed with nil by mouth, antibiotics and surgery if needed.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Vomiting in a Neonate.front: How does gastro-oesophageal reflux / posseting present, and when is it benign?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Vomiting in a Neonate.back: Effortless, non-bilious vomiting after feeds in a thriving baby; benign and self-limiting, needing only reassurance and positioning unless there is faltering growth or distress.
Vomiting with blood or mucus in the stool, eczema and faltering growth; managed with a trial of an extensively hydrolysed (hypoallergenic) formula.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Vomiting in a Neonate.front: What signs suggest vomiting is due to raised intracranial pressure?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Vomiting in a Neonate.back: A bulging fontanelle, an enlarging head circumference, drowsiness and abnormal eye movements — needs neuroimaging.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Vomiting in a Neonate.front: What is the first investigation for suspected malrotation with volvulus?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Vomiting in a Neonate.back: An urgent upper GI contrast study — do not simply observe a bilious vomiting neonate.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Failure to Thrive.front: How is failure to thrive (faltering growth) defined?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Failure to Thrive.back: A sustained fall across weight (and later length / height) centiles, or a persistently low growth velocity, plotted on growth charts.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Failure to Thrive.front: What are the four mechanistic categories of faltering growth?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Failure to Thrive.back: Inadequate intake, inadequate absorption, increased requirement / losses, and non-organic / psychosocial factors — with safeguarding considered throughout.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Failure to Thrive.front: What is the commonest cause of faltering growth?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Failure to Thrive.back: Inadequate intake — feeding technique, volumes, dilution of feeds, poverty or feeding difficulty / aversion; a careful feeding history is key.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Failure to Thrive.front: Which feature suggests coeliac disease as a cause?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Failure to Thrive.back: Diarrhoea, bloating, irritability and weight loss developing after weaning onto gluten; confirmed with anti-TTG antibodies and biopsy.
Recurrent chest infections, steatorrhoea (fatty, offensive stools) and salty sweat; confirmed by the sweat test / newborn screen.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Failure to Thrive.front: How can congenital heart disease cause faltering growth?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Failure to Thrive.back: Increased metabolic demand and breathlessness / sweating on feeds limit intake; a murmur or signs of heart failure may be present — assess with echo.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Failure to Thrive.front: What safeguarding features should prompt concern in faltering growth?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Failure to Thrive.back:
• Disengagement
  • missed appointments
  • poor hygiene
  • an inconsistent history
  • or a flat / watchful child who gains weight readily when fed in hospital.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Failure to Thrive.front: How do you distinguish faltering growth from constitutional short stature?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Failure to Thrive.back: Constitutional / familial children are small but track a low centile with a normal growth velocity and are otherwise well — not crossing centiles downwards.

• Plot weight, length / height and head circumference on growth charts
  • calculate velocity
  • perform a full systems examination and observe a feed and parent-child interaction.
Guided by history: anti-TTG (coeliac), FBC, U&E, LFTs, TFTs, urine culture, sweat test if CF suspected, and echocardiography for a murmur — avoid a blind panel.
Optimise nutrition with dietetic and feeding support, treat any underlying cause, and arrange multidisciplinary and health-visitor follow-up with growth monitoring.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Failure to Thrive.front: Why is faltering growth with loss of acquired skills concerning?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Failure to Thrive.back: It raises a metabolic or neurodegenerative disorder (developmental regression), which needs urgent neurological / metabolic investigation.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Developmental Regress.back: Regression is the LOSS of previously acquired skills (the child could do something and now cannot); delay is failure to reach milestones on time. Regression is always a red flag.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Developmental Regress.front: Which causes of regression are neurodegenerative / metabolic?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Developmental Regress.back: Leukodystrophies, storage disorders (with hepatosplenomegaly / coarse features) and mitochondrial disease; investigated with MRI and a metabolic screen.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Developmental Regress.front: What acquired brain problems can cause regression?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Developmental Regress.back: Encephalitis / meningitis, a brain tumour with raised intracranial pressure, hypoxic injury, and inflicted (abusive) head injury — all needing urgent assessment.
An epileptic encephalopathy of infancy with infantile spasms, developmental regression and hypsarrhythmia on EEG; early treatment protects development.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Developmental Regress.front: What are the features of Rett syndrome?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Developmental Regress.back: A disorder almost exclusively in girls: regression after normal early development, loss of purposeful hand use with hand-wringing stereotypies and deceleration of head growth; caused by MECP2 mutations.
Loss of language and social skills (reduced eye contact, response to name and joint attention) typically at 18-24 months; assessed by a multidisciplinary developmental team.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Developmental Regress.front: Which treatable / reversible cause of apparent regression must always be excluded?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Developmental Regress.back: Hypothyroidism (lethargy, constipation, coarse features, poor growth) — check TFTs; also treat seizures and infections.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Developmental Regress.front: What is the tempo distinction that guides investigation?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Developmental Regress.back: Acute regression (fever, seizures, drowsiness) suggests encephalitis or raised ICP; progressive loss suggests a neurodegenerative / metabolic disorder.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Developmental Regress.front: What investigations are central to working up regression?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Developmental Regress.back:
• MRI brain and EEG
  • a metabolic screen (blood / urine)
  • TFTs
  • targeted genetic testing (e.g. MECP2)
  • and LP with viral studies if encephalitis is suspected.
When there is unexplained injury, retinal haemorrhages or an inconsistent history — consider inflicted head injury and escalate.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Developmental Regress.front: What features suggest a storage disorder as the cause?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Developmental Regress.back: Regression with hepatosplenomegaly, coarse facial features and sometimes skeletal changes; investigate with metabolic / enzyme studies.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Developmental Regress.front: Why is early recognition of regression important?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Developmental Regress.back: Some causes are treatable (hypothyroidism, encephalitis, epileptic encephalopathy), and early treatment can prevent or limit permanent neurological damage.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Stridor in a Child.front: What is stridor and what does it indicate?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Stridor in a Child.back: A harsh, monophonic, usually inspiratory noise indicating upper-airway (extrathoracic) obstruction.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Stridor in a Child.front: What is the cardinal rule when epiglottitis is suspected?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Stridor in a Child.back: Keep the child calm and do NOT examine the throat or upset the child — agitation can precipitate complete airway obstruction; call senior anaesthetic / ENT help.
A toxic child sitting forward (tripod), drooling, with a muffled 'hot-potato' voice, high fever and NO cough — rapidly progressive; now rare due to Hib vaccination.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Stridor in a Child.front: What are the features and management of croup?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Stridor in a Child.back: Viral laryngotracheobronchitis (6 months-6 years, peak 6 months-3 years) with a barking (seal-like) cough, stridor, hoarseness and coryza; treated with oral dexamethasone, and nebulised adrenaline if severe.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Stridor in a Child.front: How does an inhaled foreign body present?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Stridor in a Child.back: Sudden-onset stridor or wheeze after a choking episode while eating or playing, often with focal / unilateral signs; managed by airway manoeuvres or bronchoscopic removal.
Chronic stridor from birth, worse when supine, feeding or crying, in a thriving baby; usually resolves by 18-24 months; laryngoscopy if severe.
A bacterial infection of the trachea causing high fever, toxicity and worsening stridor, often after a croup-like illness that fails to respond; needs antibiotics and airway support.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Stridor in a Child.front: What stridor plus urticaria and facial swelling indicates, and its treatment?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Stridor in a Child.back: Anaphylaxis — treated with intramuscular adrenaline, oxygen and ABC support.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Stridor in a Child.front: How is croup severity assessed at the bedside?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Stridor in a Child.back: By work of breathing, recession, stridor at rest, oxygen saturation, exhaustion and conscious level — without distressing the child.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Stridor in a Child.front: What is a retropharyngeal abscess and how does it present?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Stridor in a Child.back: A deep-neck space infection causing fever, neck pain / stiffness, reduced neck extension and drooling in a toxic child; needs imaging and ENT / surgical management.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Stridor in a Child.front: What supportive measures can be given for critical upper-airway obstruction while awaiting senior help?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Stridor in a Child.back: Oxygen and nebulised adrenaline, keeping the child calm on the parent's lap, and preparing for a controlled airway with anaesthetics / ENT.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Stridor in a Child.front: Which congenital anomalies cause persistent / recurrent stridor?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Stridor in a Child.back: Vascular ring, subglottic stenosis and laryngeal web / cyst, often with feeding difficulty from birth; assessed by laryngobronchoscopy.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Wheeze in a Child.front: What is wheeze and where is the obstruction?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Wheeze in a Child.back: A high-pitched, usually expiratory, polyphonic noise from lower-airway (intrathoracic) narrowing.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Wheeze in a Child.front: Why is a silent chest in a wheezy child alarming?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Wheeze in a Child.back: The wheeze can disappear as air entry fails — a silent chest signals life-threatening asthma, not improvement.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Wheeze in a Child.front: What are the features of life-threatening asthma in a child?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Wheeze in a Child.back: Silent chest, cyanosis, poor respiratory effort / exhaustion, SpO₂ <92%, hypotension and altered consciousness — treat immediately and escalate.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Wheeze in a Child.front: What is bronchiolitis and who does it affect?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Wheeze in a Child.back: A viral (usually RSV) lower-airway infection in infants under 1 year, causing coryza then wheeze, fine crackles, increased work of breathing, poor feeding and apnoeas; management is supportive.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Wheeze in a Child.front: Why do bronchodilators often fail in bronchiolitis and preschool viral wheeze?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Wheeze in a Child.back: The airway obstruction in these young children is not primarily bronchospasm, so beta-agonists frequently have little effect.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Wheeze in a Child.front: What features suggest asthma rather than a one-off wheeze?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Wheeze in a Child.back: Episodic wheeze and cough worse at night or with exercise, identifiable triggers, atopy and a family history of atopy, with symptom-free periods.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Wheeze in a Child.front: What wheeze plus systemic features signals anaphylaxis, and its treatment?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Wheeze in a Child.back: Wheeze with urticaria, facial / lip swelling or hypotension after an allergen — treated with IM adrenaline.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Wheeze in a Child.front: When should an inhaled foreign body be suspected in a wheezy child?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Wheeze in a Child.back: When wheeze starts suddenly after a choking episode or is focal / unilateral; confirmed and treated by bronchoscopy.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Wheeze in a Child.front: Which chronic condition presents with recurrent wheeze, wet cough and faltering growth?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Wheeze in a Child.back: Cystic fibrosis (with steatorrhoea and recurrent infections); confirmed by the sweat test / newborn screen.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Wheeze in a Child.front: What is the immediate management of an acute severe / life-threatening asthma attack?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Wheeze in a Child.back: Oxygen to keep SpO₂ ≥94%, back-to-back inhaled / nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, oral or IV steroids, and escalation (IV magnesium / salbutamol, seniors / ICU).
Supportive care: monitoring, oxygen if hypoxic and feeding support (NG or IV fluids); most cases are self-limiting, with high-risk infants admitted.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Wheeze in a Child.front: What rare cardiac cause can produce wheeze in an infant?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Wheeze in a Child.back: Heart failure from congenital heart disease ('cardiac wheeze') — suspect with poor feeding, sweating, hepatomegaly and a murmur; assess with echocardiography.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__The Floppy Infant.front: What is the floppy infant and what is the key first distinction?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__The Floppy Infant.back: An infant with reduced muscle tone (hypotonia — head lag, frog-leg posture); the first step is to distinguish central (brain) from peripheral (nerve / muscle) causes.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__The Floppy Infant.front: How do central and peripheral hypotonia differ clinically?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__The Floppy Infant.back: Central: reduced alertness with preserved / brisk reflexes.Peripheral (anterior horn cell to muscle): an alert baby with weakness and reduced / absent reflexes.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__The Floppy Infant.front: Why must an acutely floppy, unwell infant be treated as an emergency?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__The Floppy Infant.back: Sepsis or meningitis can present as acute floppiness with poor feeding, temperature instability or apnoea — screen and give antibiotics without delay.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__The Floppy Infant.front: What are the features of spinal muscular atrophy type 1?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__The Floppy Infant.back: An alert infant with progressive weakness, areflexia, tongue fasciculations, a bell-shaped chest and paradoxical breathing; caused by SMN1 mutations, with time-critical disease-modifying therapy.
Brain injury from perinatal asphyxia causing a depressed, floppy neonate with acidosis, seizures and multi-organ involvement; treated with therapeutic cooling.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__The Floppy Infant.front: What features suggest Down syndrome in a floppy infant?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__The Floppy Infant.back: Central hypotonia with dysmorphism — flat facial profile, upslanting palpebral fissures, single palmar crease — and associated cardiac / duodenal anomalies; confirmed by karyotype.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__The Floppy Infant.front: How does Prader-Willi syndrome present in infancy?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__The Floppy Infant.back: Severe central hypotonia with poor feeding and hypogonadism in infancy, followed later by hyperphagia and obesity; confirmed by methylation studies.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__The Floppy Infant.front: Which peripheral neuromuscular causes present as a floppy baby?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__The Floppy Infant.back: Congenital myotonic dystrophy (floppy baby with a myotonic mother), congenital myopathies and neonatal myasthenia (fatigable weakness with a myasthenic mother).

signs__PAEDIATRIC__The Floppy Infant.front: Which treatable endocrine cause of a floppy infant must be excluded?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__The Floppy Infant.back: Congenital hypothyroidism (prolonged jaundice, constipation, coarse features, poor feeding) — check the newborn screen / TFTs and treat with thyroxine.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__The Floppy Infant.front: What is the sign of a peripheral cause in an alert floppy baby with tongue fasciculations?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__The Floppy Infant.back: It points strongly to spinal muscular atrophy (anterior horn cell disease).

signs__PAEDIATRIC__The Floppy Infant.front: What investigations are guided by the central vs peripheral split?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__The Floppy Infant.back:
Septic screen if unwell; then
  • SMN1 genetics
  • karyotype
  • methylation studies
  • TFTs
  • CK
  • EMG
  • MRI brain and metabolic studies as indicated.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__The Floppy Infant.front: When is safeguarding relevant in a floppy infant?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__The Floppy Infant.back: When floppiness is accompanied by unexplained injury or retinal haemorrhages, raising inflicted (abusive) head injury.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Neonatal Jaundice.front: Why is the timing of neonatal jaundice so important?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Neonatal Jaundice.back:
Timing directs the differential:
  • <24 hours is always pathological
  • day 2-14 in a well term baby is usually physiological
  • and prolonged jaundice must be fractionated into conjugated vs unconjugated.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Neonatal Jaundice.front: What does jaundice in the first 24 hours of life indicate?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Neonatal Jaundice.back: It is always pathological — haemolysis (rhesus / ABO incompatibility, G6PD deficiency, spherocytosis) or congenital infection / sepsis until proven otherwise.

Acute bilirubin encephalopathy from very high unconjugated bilirubin crossing the blood-brain barrier, causing lethargy, a high-pitched cry, hypertonia and arching (opisthotonus), with permanent brain injury.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Neonatal Jaundice.front: What is the significance of prolonged jaundice with pale stools and dark urine?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Neonatal Jaundice.back: It indicates conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia from biliary atresia until proven otherwise — needs early diagnosis and a Kasai portoenterostomy (ideally before 60 days).
Jaundice persisting beyond 14 days in a term baby (or 21 days in a preterm baby).

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Neonatal Jaundice.front: What are the causes of prolonged unconjugated jaundice?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Neonatal Jaundice.back: Breast-milk jaundice, hypothyroidism, urinary tract infection and ongoing haemolysis (e.g. G6PD deficiency).
Unconjugated jaundice appearing after 24 hours (typically day 2-4) in a well term baby, resolving within about 2 weeks.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Neonatal Jaundice.front: How is bilirubin used to guide treatment?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Neonatal Jaundice.back: Serum bilirubin is plotted against gestation- and age-specific treatment threshold charts to decide on phototherapy or exchange transfusion.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Neonatal Jaundice.front: What investigations are needed for early or severe jaundice?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Neonatal Jaundice.back:
• Serum (and split) bilirubin
  • FBC and blood film
  • blood group and DAT (Coombs)
  • G6PD level
  • and a septic screen if the baby is unwell.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Neonatal Jaundice.front: Why must any jaundiced, unwell neonate be screened for sepsis?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Neonatal Jaundice.back: Jaundice can be the presenting sign of infection (including UTI); a septic screen and antibiotics are needed if the baby is unwell.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Neonatal Jaundice.front: What is the treatment for dangerously high unconjugated bilirubin?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Neonatal Jaundice.back: Intensive phototherapy and, above the exchange threshold or with signs of encephalopathy, an exchange transfusion.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Neonatal Jaundice.front: Which prolonged-jaundice screen is used to avoid missing biliary atresia?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Neonatal Jaundice.back: A split (conjugated / unconjugated) bilirubin — a raised conjugated fraction with pale stools mandates urgent hepatobiliary assessment (USS, and referral for possible Kasai).

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Seizures & Funny Turn.front: What most reliably distinguishes epileptic seizures from non-epileptic events in children?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Seizures & Funny Turn.back: A detailed eye-witness account of before (trigger, prodrome, posture), during (movements, duration, colour, tongue-biting, incontinence) and after (post-ictal drowsiness vs rapid recovery).

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Seizures & Funny Turn.front: What must you assume in a child who seizes with fever and looks unwell?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Seizures & Funny Turn.back: Meningitis or encephalitis until proven otherwise — do not assume a simple febrile convulsion in a drowsy, toxic or focal child; perform an LP and give antibiotics ± aciclovir.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Seizures & Funny Turn.front: What is the one bedside test to perform in every seizing child?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Seizures & Funny Turn.back: A bedside blood glucose — hypoglycaemia is a rapidly reversible cause of seizures.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Seizures & Funny Turn.front: How is status epilepticus defined and managed?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Seizures & Funny Turn.back: A seizure lasting 5 minutes or more or recurrent seizures without recovery; managed with ABC, oxygen, glucose and a benzodiazepine following the APLS algorithm, with escalation.
A brief (<15 min), generalised seizure with a fever in a child aged 6 months-5 years, who recovers fully and has no recurrence within 24 hours; it is otherwise a well child.
A tendency to recurrent unprovoked seizures (tonic-clonic, focal, absence or myoclonic); investigated with EEG and sometimes MRI.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Seizures & Funny Turn.front: What are reflex anoxic seizures and breath-holding spells?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Seizures & Funny Turn.back: Benign provoked events: reflex anoxic seizures follow a sudden pain / fright (pallor then brief stiffening); breath-holding spells follow crying (a cyanotic pause), both with quick recovery.
A faint when upright, with a prodrome (light-headedness, nausea, visual greying), pallor and rapid, complete recovery on lying flat; brief jerks may occur but it is not epilepsy.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Seizures & Funny Turn.front: When does a seizure / funny turn raise safeguarding concern?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Seizures & Funny Turn.back: An unexplained seizure or apnoea in an infant, particularly with retinal haemorrhages or an inconsistent history — consider inflicted (abusive) head injury.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Seizures & Funny Turn.front: What suggests raised intracranial pressure as a cause of seizures?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Seizures & Funny Turn.back: Early-morning headache and vomiting, a new focal seizure or neurological signs, and papilloedema — image the brain.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Seizures & Funny Turn.front: What features during an event support a true epileptic seizure over syncope?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Seizures & Funny Turn.back: Lack of a clear trigger, tongue-biting (lateral), incontinence, prolonged post-ictal drowsiness and cyanosis, rather than a rapid recovery.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Seizures & Funny Turn.front: What is the general approach to a first afebrile seizure in a well child?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Seizures & Funny Turn.back: Take a careful history, check glucose, examine fully, and refer for outpatient assessment (EEG ± MRI) with safety-netting; not all first seizures need admission if the child is well and recovered.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Constipation in a Chi.front: What is the commonest cause of constipation in a child?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Constipation in a Chi.back: Functional (idiopathic) constipation — hard, painful, infrequent stools with a withholding cycle in an otherwise well, thriving child.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Constipation in a Chi.front: Which red flag points to Hirschsprung’s disease?
signs__PAEDIATRIC__Constipation in a Chi.back: Delayed passage of meconium (>48 hours) and constipation from birth, often with abdominal distension, bilious vomiting and ribbon stools.
Suction rectal biopsy showing absence of ganglion cells (aganglionosis); an abdominal X-ray and contrast enema support it.

signs__PAEDIATRIC__Constipation in a Chi.front: What is overflow soiling and why does it matter?
